topic: Earth in the Solar System & Its Motions

items.title: The Solar System — Origin, Members & Planets
items.body:
The **solar system** is gravitationally bound to the **Sun** and comprises **eight planets**, dwarf planets, moons, and millions of asteroids, comets and meteoroids. Per the **Nebular Hypothesis** (Kant–Laplace), a collapsing cloud of dust and gas formed the Sun (~99.9% of matter) and, from the leftover **protoplanetary disc**, the planets grew by **accretion** — all about **4.6 billion years ago**.

Planets fall into two groups:

| Group | Planets | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Terrestrial (inner) | Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars | Small, rocky, dense, few moons |
| Jovian (outer) | Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune | Large, gaseous, many moons |

The **asteroid belt** (Mars–Jupiter) separates the two. Uranus and Neptune are 'ice giants'. Beyond Neptune lies the **Kuiper Belt** (30–50 AU, home to Pluto) and, far out, the **Oort Cloud** (source of long-period comets). 1 AU ≈ 150 million km.
keyPoints: Solar system = Sun + 8 planets + dwarf planets + moons + asteroids + comets + meteoroids.
Nebular Hypothesis (Kant–Laplace): Sun took ~99.9% of the collapsing nebula's matter, formed ~4.6 billion years ago.
Terrestrial (inner) planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — small, rocky, dense.
Jovian (outer) planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — large, gaseous; Uranus & Neptune are ice giants.
Asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter; Kuiper Belt (30–50 AU) beyond Neptune; Oort Cloud is the comet source.
1 Astronomical Unit (AU) ≈ 150 million km.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — World Geography: Stars and The Solar System

items.title: Distinctive Planet & Small-Body Facts
items.body:
APPSC frequently tests 'odd-one-out' planet facts:

- **Mercury** — smallest planet, closest to the Sun; extreme diurnal range (−173°C to 427°C).
- **Venus** — brightest planet, **hottest** (runaway greenhouse, ~96% CO₂), **retrograde** (clockwise) spin; a day (243 days) is **longer than its year** (225 days); 'Earth's twin'.
- **Mars** — 'Red Planet' (iron oxide); two moons; thin CO₂ atmosphere.
- **Jupiter** — largest planet; Galilean moons (Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto); **Ganymede** is the largest moon in the solar system.
- **Saturn** — famous ring system; **Titan** (only moon with a substantial N₂ atmosphere).
- **Uranus** — axis nearly in its orbital plane (rolls on its side); retrograde.
- **Neptune** — **strongest winds** (~2,100 km/h).

**IAU dwarf planet** = orbits the Sun, is round, but has **not cleared its orbit** → Pluto, Eris (Kuiper Belt), Ceres (largest asteroid). **Comets** have highly elliptical orbits (Halley's ≈ every 76 years). **Meteoroid** (rock in space) → **meteor** (streak on entry) → **meteorite** (survives to the ground).
keyPoints: Venus: hottest planet, retrograde spin, day longer than year, densest terrestrial atmosphere.
Mercury: smallest, closest to Sun, greatest day–night temperature range.
Jupiter largest; Ganymede (its moon) is the biggest moon in the solar system, larger than Mercury.
Neptune has the fastest planetary winds (~2,100 km/h); Uranus's axis lies almost in its orbital plane.
Dwarf planet fails only the 'cleared its orbit' criterion — e.g. Pluto, Eris, Ceres.
Meteoroid → meteor (shooting star) → meteorite (reaches surface); comets have highly elliptical orbits.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — World Geography: Stars and The Solar System

items.title: The Sun, the Moon & Eclipses
items.body:
The **Sun** is a star of mainly **hydrogen (~75%)** and **helium (~24%)**; its mass is **~99.86%** of the solar system. Energy comes from **hydrogen→helium fusion** in the core; light takes **8 min 20 s** to reach Earth. Layers (in→out): core, radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere, chromosphere, corona. **Sunspots** are *cooler*, darker patches; **solar wind** and **solar flares** are other activity.

The **Moon** shines by reflecting sunlight; its **phases** cycle every **~29 days** (waxing/waning). It likely formed from a **giant impact ('big splat')** on the early Earth.

**Eclipses**:

| Type | Geometry | Occurs on |
|---|---|---|
| Lunar | Earth between Sun & Moon | Full Moon |
| Solar | Moon between Sun & Earth | New Moon |

Shadow terms: **umbra** (total), **penumbra** (partial), **antumbra** (annular 'ring of fire'). The **Saros cycle** (~18 yr 11 d) governs eclipse repetition.
keyPoints: Sun: ~75% hydrogen, ~24% helium; ~99.86% of the solar system's mass; sunlight reaches Earth in 8 min 20 s.
Sunspots are cooler (darker) patches on the photosphere; energy = core nuclear fusion.
Moon reflects sunlight; phases repeat ~every 29 days; formed by a giant impact ('big splat').
Lunar eclipse: Earth between Sun and Moon, only on a Full Moon; Solar eclipse: Moon between Sun and Earth, only on a New Moon.
Umbra = total, penumbra = partial, antumbra = annular 'ring of fire'.
Saros cycle ≈ 18 years 11 days for eclipse repetition.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — World Geography: Stars and The Solar System

items.title: Earth's Motions — Rotation, Revolution & Seasons
items.body:
Earth has two motions:

- **Rotation** — spins west→east on its axis in ~**24 hours** (≈23h56m sidereal), giving **day and night**. The axis is inclined **66½°** to the orbital plane (i.e. **23½° from the vertical**); the **circle of illumination** (day–night boundary) therefore does not coincide with the axis. Rotation also causes the **Coriolis effect**, deflecting winds/currents right in the NH and left in the SH.
- **Revolution** — orbits the Sun in an **elliptical** path in **365¼ days**; the spare ~6 hours/year give a **leap year** (366 days) every 4 years. Nearest point = **perihelion** (~Jan), farthest = **aphelion** (~Jul).

**Seasons** arise from the 23½° tilt + revolution:

| Event | Date | Sun overhead | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Summer solstice | 21 Jun | Tropic of Cancer | Longest NH day; Arctic Circle 24-h daylight |
| Winter solstice | 22 Dec | Tropic of Capricorn | Longest SH day; Antarctic 24-h daylight |
| Equinoxes | 21 Mar & 23 Sep | Equator | Day = night everywhere |

The **poles** get ~6 months of continuous day, then ~6 months of night.
keyPoints: Rotation: west→east, ~24 h, axis tilted 66½° to orbital plane (23½° from vertical) → day/night + Coriolis effect.
Circle of illumination (day–night line) does not align with the axis because of the tilt.
Revolution: elliptical orbit in 365¼ days → leap year (366 days) every 4 years; perihelion ~Jan, aphelion ~Jul.
Summer solstice 21 Jun — Sun over Tropic of Cancer, longest NH day; winter solstice 22 Dec — Sun over Tropic of Capricorn.
Equinoxes 21 Mar & 23 Sep — Sun over the equator, equal day and night worldwide.
Poles experience about six months of daylight followed by six months of darkness.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — World Geography: Motions of the Earth

items.title: Latitudes, Longitudes, Heat Zones & Time
items.body:
**Latitudes** are parallels measured 0°–90° N/S from the **equator (0°)**; 1° ≈ **111 km**. Key parallels: **Tropic of Cancer 23½°N**, **Tropic of Capricorn 23½°S**, **Arctic Circle 66½°N**, **Antarctic Circle 66½°S**, poles 90°.

**Heat zones**: **Torrid** (23½°N–23½°S, overhead sun), **Temperate** (tropics↔polar circles), **Frigid** (polar circles↔poles).

**Longitudes** are meridians 0°–180° E/W of the **Prime Meridian (Greenwich, 0°)** — 360 in all; they converge at the poles. The **International Date Line** roughly follows 180°.

**Longitude & time**: Earth turns **15°/hour** (**1° = 4 minutes**). Places east of Greenwich are ahead, west are behind. India uses **82½°E** as its standard meridian, so **IST = GMT + 5:30**.
keyPoints: Latitudes run 0°–90° N/S from the equator; 1° of latitude ≈ 111 km.
Tropic of Cancer 23½°N, Tropic of Capricorn 23½°S, Arctic Circle 66½°N, Antarctic Circle 66½°S.
Heat zones: Torrid (between the tropics), Temperate (tropics to polar circles), Frigid (polar circles to poles).
Longitudes: 0°–180° E/W of the Prime Meridian (Greenwich); 360 meridians; IDL ≈ 180°.
Earth rotates 15° of longitude per hour (1° = 4 minutes); east of Greenwich is ahead in time.
India's standard meridian is 82½°E, so IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

items.title: Astronomy Basics — Eclipses, Seasons, Dwarf Planets & Time
items.body:
## Eclipses

- **Solar eclipse** — on a **new moon**, when the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth. Total (umbra), partial (penumbra), annular 'ring of fire' (antumbra, Moon far and small).
- **Lunar eclipse** — on a **full moon**, when the Earth comes between the Sun and Moon.
- Eclipses are **not monthly** because the Moon's orbit is tilted ~**5°** to the ecliptic; they occur only when a new/full moon falls near a **node** (where the planes cross).

## Seasons

- Caused by the **23½° axial tilt**, not by Earth–Sun distance. Proof: Earth is at **aphelion** (farthest, ~152 M km) in early **July**, yet the Northern Hemisphere has summer.
- **Perihelion** (nearest, ~147 M km) ≈ 3 January. Opposite hemispheres always have opposite seasons.
- Solstices: 21 Jun (Sun over Tropic of Cancer, longest NH day) and 22 Dec (Tropic of Capricorn). Equinoxes: 21 Mar and 23 Sep (Sun over Equator, day = night everywhere).

## Dwarf planets (IAU)

Five recognised: **Ceres** (asteroid belt) and **Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake** (beyond Neptune). A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is round but has **not cleared its orbit**. (Charon is Pluto's moon, not a dwarf planet.)

## Longitude & time

- Earth turns **15° per hour → 1° = 4 minutes**. Places **east** of a reference meridian are **ahead**.
- Example: at 82½°E (IST) it is 10:00 AM → Kohima (94°E) is 11½° × 4 = 46 min ahead = **10:46 AM**.
- IST = GMT + 5:30 (82½°E). International Date Line ≈ 180°.
keyPoints: Solar eclipse on new moon (Moon between Sun and Earth); lunar eclipse on full moon (Earth between Sun and Moon).
Eclipses are not monthly because the Moon's orbit tilts ~5°; they need a new/full moon near a node.
Seasons are caused by the 23½° axial tilt, not the Earth–Sun distance.
Earth is at aphelion (~152 M km) in early July and perihelion (~147 M km) in early January.
IAU recognises five dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake (Charon is a moon).
15° longitude = 1 hour, 1° = 4 minutes; places east of the reference meridian are ahead in time.
IST is based on 82½°E and is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
items.mnemonic: Solar = New moon (both start with the Sun's shadow on us); Lunar = fuLL moon.
items.source: International Astronomical Union (IAU); local APPSC GK PDF — World Geography: Motions of the Earth; Latitudes & Longitudes; Stars and The Solar System

items.title: High-yield Named Facts — Habitable Zone, Early Earth & Sky Navigation
items.body:
A cluster of recurring prelims facts that sit outside the core motions/seasons material:

## Goldilocks (habitable) zone

- The **habitable or 'Goldilocks' zone** is the orbital band around a star where temperatures allow **liquid water** on a planet — 'just right', neither too hot nor too cold.
- Seen in the news in the context of the **search for Earth-like exoplanets** (Kepler/TESS).

## Early Earth & its atmosphere

- Earth is **~4.6 billion years** old. Its **early atmosphere had almost no free oxygen** (mostly CO₂, methane, water vapour, nitrogen).
- **Free O₂ accumulated later** through **photosynthesis by early organisms** (Great Oxidation Event ~2.4 bya) — life *modified* the atmosphere.
- Earth's **magnetic field reverses polarity** episodically over geological time; the record is frozen as symmetric **paleomagnetic stripes** across mid-ocean ridges.

## Earth-shaping (dynamic-change) agents

- Agents that bring dynamic change to the surface: **geothermal energy, plate movements, and the Earth's rotation and revolution** (endogenic + motion-driven).
- Solar radiation powers weathering/erosion, but rotation (Coriolis) and revolution (seasonal insolation) are the motion agents tested in PYQs.

## Sky navigation

- The **Pole Star (Polaris / Dhruva)** lies almost above the north celestial pole, so it barely moves — a guide to **true north**.
- Found using the **pointer stars (Merak, Dubhe) of Ursa Major (Saptarishi / Great Bear)**.
keyPoints: The Goldilocks/habitable zone is the orbit around a star where liquid water can exist — context: search for Earth-like exoplanets.
Earth's early atmosphere had no free oxygen; O₂ built up later from photosynthesis by early life (life modified the atmosphere).
Earth's magnetic field reverses polarity over geological time, recorded as paleomagnetic stripes across mid-ocean ridges.
Dynamic surface-change agents: geothermal energy, plate movements, Earth's rotation and revolution.
The Pole Star (Polaris) marks true north; it is located using the pointer stars of Ursa Major (Saptarishi).
items.source: UPSC CSE Prelims 2013/2015/2018; NCERT Fundamentals of Physical Geography; local APPSC GK PDF — Stars and the Solar System
